label: Single-chambered foraminiferal shells take the form of fluid drops under surface tension
claim: The form of a single-chambered foraminiferal shell is explained by the laws of surface tension: the protoplasm behaves as a fluid drop whose equilibrium shape is fixed when it acquires its solid covering.
quote: wherever the shell is but a single unit or single chamber, its form may be explained in general by the laws of surface tension: the assumption being that the little mass of protoplasm which makes the simple shell behaves as a _fluid drop_, the form of which is perpetuated when the protoplasm acquires its solid covering.

label: Foraminifera are spiral because they grow by permanent increments added outside
claim: Foraminiferal shells tend towards a spiral form because they grow by successive increments added to the exterior, each of which becomes a permanent, rigid part of the structure.
quote: That the shell in the Foraminifera should tend towards a spiral form need not surprise us; for we have learned that one of the fundamental conditions of the production of a concrete spiral is just precisely what we have here, namely the gradual development of a structure by means of successive increments superadded to its exterior, which then form part, successively, of a permanent and rigid structure.

label: Septa are convex outwards in Foraminifera and concave in Nautilus because of pressure side
claim: Foraminiferal septa are convex outwards and those of Nautilus concave outwards because the pressure each membrane resisted when it set lay on opposite sides; in both cases the septum tends to a surface of minimal area.
quote: The one septum is, speaking generally, the reverse of the other; the organism, so to speak, is outside the one and inside the other; and in both cases alike, the septum tends to assume the form of a surface of minimal area, as permitted, or as defined, by all the circumstances of the case.
scope: septa of chambered Foraminifera and chambered cephalopod shells

label: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, large shells similar to small ones
claim: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, recognisable by continued similarity: the large many-chambered shell has the same shape as the smaller, younger shell.
quote: The logarithmic spiral is easily recognisable in typical cases (and especially where the spire makes more than one visible revolution about the pole), by its fundamental property of continued similarity: that is to say, by reason of the fact that the big many-chambered shell is of just the same shape as the smaller and younger shell

label: Fusulina whorls increase in ratio 1:1.5, a spiral of constant angle about 86°
claim: In Fusulina the breadths of successive whorls stand in the nearly constant ratio 1 : 1.5, which corresponds to a logarithmic spiral with a constant angle of about 86°, like that of ammonites.
quote: And this ratio of 1·5 between the breadths of successive whorls corresponds (as we see by our table on p. 534) to a constant angle of about 86°, or just such a spiral as we commonly meet with in the Ammonites

label: Constant chamber-size ratio follows from growth proportional to existing mass
claim: Each foraminiferal chamber bears a constant ratio of size to the next because the rate of increase at each instant is proportional to the whole existing mass of the homogeneous organism.
quote: The law of increase by which each chamber bears a constant ratio of magnitude to the next may be looked upon as a simple consequence of the structural uniformity or homogeneity of the organism; we have merely to suppose (as this uniformity would naturally lead us to do) that the rate of increase is at each instant proportional to the whole existing mass.

label: Minimum potential energy plus proportional growth yields the logarithmic spiral
claim: Each new protoplasmic drop settles in a position of minimum potential energy (including minimal area), which makes each chamber similar to the last; proportional growth of size then gives the series the form of a logarithmic spiral. Rhumbler's specific 'law of the constant angle' of contact is too narrow an explanation.
quote: The physical law of minimum potential (including also the law of minimal area) is all that we need in order to explain, _in general terms_, the continued similarity of one chamber to another; and the physiological law of growth, by which a continued proportionality of size tends to run through the series of successive chambers, impresses upon this series of similar increments the form of a logarithmic spiral.

label: Attached Foraminifera form plane spirals with whorls flattened on the attached side
claim: Most spiral Foraminifera are plane (discoid) spirals because some force keeps the chambers in a plane, especially in forms that live attached to rock or seaweed, whose whorls are flattened on the attached surface; freely floating forms such as Globigerina tend towards helicoid spirals.
quote: The majority of spiral forms, on the other hand, are plane or discoid spirals, and we may take it that in these cases some force has exercised a controlling influence, so as to keep all the chambers in a plane. This is especially the case in forms like Rotalia or Discorbina (Fig. 316), where the organism lives attached to a rock or a frond of sea-weed

label: Many foraminiferal species and genera may be temporary manifestations of variability
claim: Because very slight changes in surface energies could turn one foraminiferal form into another, many forms distinguished as separate species and even genera may be no more than temporary manifestations of variability, as in Peneroplis.
quote: but for all we know of the life-history of the Foraminifera, it may well be that a great number of the other forms which we distinguish as separate species and even genera are no more than temporary manifestations of the same variability
section: Variability and the constancy of species

label: Foraminiferal forms follow such simple laws that none is fitter than another to survive
claim: Foraminiferal shells grow by laws so simple and so in harmony with their material and the forces acting on them that no form is better, fitter or less fit to survive than another, which accounts for the great diversity of types and their persistence since the Cretaceous.
quote: It leads one to imagine that these shells have grown according to laws so simple, so much in harmony with their material, with their environment, and with all the forces internal and external to which they are exposed, that none is better than another and none fitter or less fit to survive.

label: Identical foraminiferal forms may have arisen independently again and again
claim: The possible lines of variation in Foraminifera may be so narrow and determinate that identical forms have arisen independently many times.
quote: It invites one also to contemplate the possibility of the lines of possible variation being here so narrow and determinate that identical forms may have come independently into being again and again.

label: Increased shell strength is not an advantage driving foraminiferal evolution
claim: Against Rhumbler, niceties of shell form have little effect on survival: delicate foraminiferal shells survive unbroken in vast numbers, so breakage is not a constant danger and increased strength is not a selective advantage guiding their evolution.
quote: And so I am not inclined to believe that niceties of form affect the case very much: nor in general that foraminiferal life involves a struggle for existence wherein breakage is a constant danger to be averted, and increased strength an advantage to be ensured.
section: Strength as a supposed selective factor

label: Foraminifera are absent from coarse gravels because of hydraulic sorting by currents
claim: Foraminiferal shells are absent from coarse sands and gravels not because they avoid concussion but because light shells are sorted by currents like any other graded sediment, settling where water is still.
quote: The coarseness or fineness of the sediment on the sea-bottom is a measure of the current: where the current is strong the larger stones are washed clean, where there is perfect stillness the finest mud settles down; and the light, fragile shells of the Foraminifera find their appropriate place, like every other graded sediment, in this spontaneous order of lixiviation.
section: Strength as a supposed selective factor

label: Forms set by physical forces undermine inference of kinship from similarity
claim: Insofar as forms depend on physical forces and their variations on simple quantitative changes in those forces, similarity of form cannot safely be taken as evidence of consanguinity, and the link between classification and phylogeny must be revised.
quote: But in so far as forms can be shewn to depend on the play of physical forces, and the variations of form to be directly due to simple quantitative variations in these, just so far are we thrown back on our guard before the biological conception of consanguinity, and compelled to revise the vague canons which connect classification with phylogeny.
scope: Foraminifera and other organisms whose form is governed by physical forces

label: Rhinoceros horn is a plane logarithmic spiral from constant front-to-back growth ratio
claim: The rhinoceros horn grows faster anteriorly than posteriorly in a constant ratio, so it curves as a logarithmic spiral; lying in the median plane, it has no lateral twist and forms a plane spiral.
quote: Its longitudinal growth proceeds with a maximum velocity anteriorly, and a minimum posteriorly; and the ratio of these velocities being constant, the horn curves into the form of a logarithmic spiral in the manner that we have already studied.

label: Paired horns of ruminants are conjugate, mirror-image spirals
claim: The paired horns of hollow-horned ruminants are conjugate spirals, the left horn being the mirror image of the right.
quote: But the two horns are in symmetry one with another; they form “conjugate” spirals, one being the “mirror-image” of the other.

label: Most horns are logarithmic spirals from constant unequal growth on opposite sides
claim: In the great majority of horns the curve is a continuous logarithmic spiral, caused by unequal rates of growth parallel to the axis on opposite sides of the horn, the inequality keeping a constant ratio throughout growth.
quote: But in the great majority of horns, we have no difficulty in recognising a continuous logarithmic spiral, nor in referring it, as before, to an unequal rate of growth (parallel to the axis) on two opposite sides of the horn, the inequality maintaining a constant ratio as long as growth proceeds.

label: Goat and sheep horns form a series of homologous spirals of increasing angle
claim: Horns of wild goats and sheep form a series of homologous logarithmic spirals with increasing constant angle: under 40° in Oryx, under 70° in the Scinde wild goat, about 75° in Ovis ammon and a little more in the Highland ram.
quote: we may easily arrange a series of forms, such for example as the Siberian ibex, the moufflon, _Ovis Ammon_, etc., and ending with the long-horned Highland ram: in which, as we pass from one to another, we recognise precisely homologous spirals, with an increasing angular constant, the spiral angle being, for instance, about 75° or rather less in _Ovis Ammon_, and in the Highland ram a very little more.
scope: horns of Oryx, Capra and Ovis species

label: Argali horns share a spiral angle but differ in their shearing (helical) component
claim: Among closely allied wild sheep (Argali) the constant angle of the horn's logarithmic spiral is nearly the same, and the species differ chiefly in the helical shearing component.
quote: In all of these the constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is very much the same, but the shearing component differs greatly.
scope: Asiatic wild sheep (Ovis ammon, O. poli, O. hodgsoni)

label: A horn is a plane spiral only if fastest and slowest growth lie diametrically opposite
claim: If the maximal and minimal growth rates around the basal growth zone of a horn lie diametrically opposite, the horn is a plane spiral; otherwise it is a spiral in space with a helical component, which is the usual case because the horn's field of force has no such plane of symmetry.
quote: If the maximal and minimal velocities of growth be precisely at opposite sides of the zone of growth, the resultant spiral will be a plane spiral; but if they be not precisely or diametrically opposite, then the spiral will be a spiral in space, with a winding or helical component

label: Uneven adhesion of the horn sheath to its bony core can itself produce the spiral
claim: Unequal retardation of the growing horn sheath by its adhesion to the bony core can produce the same spiral as unequal growth, and is probably a very important and sometimes the chief factor in horn curvature.
quote: had its elongation more retarded on one side than the other (prior to its complete solidification) by varying degrees of adhesion or membranous attachment to the bone core within, then the net result would be a spiral curve precisely such as would have arisen from initial inequalities in the rate of growth itself. It seems highly probable that this is a very important factor

label: The thicker the horn, the greater its spiral curvature
claim: On the whole, thicker horns are more strongly spirally curved than slender ones, because a larger cross-section allows greater differences in growth or retardation between opposite sides.
quote: I think it may be said that, on the whole, the thicker the horn, the greater is its spiral curvature.
scope: horns of antelopes, goats and sheep

label: Sinuous growth lines on non-cylindrical horns result from torsional strain
claim: Horns that grow as curves of double curvature undergo torsional strain, because the sheath is attached to the core, and this strain warps the rings into the sinuous growth lines predicted by St Venant for a twisted non-circular prism; such lines are absent from cylindrical ox horns.
quote: But there is yet another and a very remarkable phenomenon which we may discern in the growth of a horn, when it takes the form of a curve of double curvature, namely, an effect of torsional strain; and this it is which gives rise to the sinuous “lines of growth,” or sinuous boundaries of the separate horny rings, of which we have already spoken.
section: Torsion and growth lines of horns
scope: horns of sheep, Ovis ammon, antelopes; contrasted with oxen

label: Twining of climbing stems results from unequal growth on different sides
claim: The revolving nutation of twining plants, like the helicoid growth of an antelope horn, is caused by unequal rates of growth on different sides of the stem, the difference being that in the stem growth occurs along its whole length.
quote: This tendency to revolution—“circumvolution,” as Darwin calls it, “revolving nutation,” as Sachs puts it—is very closely comparable to the process by which an antelope’s horn (such as the koodoo’s) grows into its spiral or rather helicoid form; and it is simply due, in like manner, to inequalities in the rate of growth on different sides of the growing stem.

label: Stem torsion on rough supports is a mechanical couple from adhesion, not an adaptation
claim: Twining stems become twisted on rough supports but not on smooth ones because adhesion to the rough support sets up a mechanical couple, so Darwin's adaptive explanation (gaining rigidity) is unnecessary.
quote: In the case of the roughened support, there is a temporary adhesion or “clinging” between it and the growing stem which twines around it; and a system of forces is thus set up, producing a “couple,” just as it was in the case of the ram’s or antelope’s horn through direct adhesion of the bony core to the surrounding sheath.

label: A pair of antlers is confined to a single smooth spheroidal surface
claim: The branches of a pair of deer antlers are confined to a single, more or less spheroidal or ellipsoidal curved surface, the two antlers forming one mirror-symmetric surface whose tine tips lie on a continuous curve; the antler is essentially a surface, whereas a horn is an axial rod.
quote: The surface to which the branches of the antler tend to be confined is a more or less spheroidal, or occasionally an ellipsoidal one; and furthermore, when we inspect any well-developed pair of antlers, such as those of a red deer, a sambur or a wapiti, we have no difficulty in seeing that the two antlers make up between them _a single surface_

label: Claws, beaks and teeth grown by unequal permanent accretion are logarithmic spirals
claim: Wherever a structure grows by permanent increments with unequal longitudinal growth about its axis, as in nails, claws, beaks and teeth, it always tends to the form of a logarithmic spiral, which becomes conspicuous only when the structure is long.
quote: The logarithmic spiral _always_ tends to manifest itself in such structures as these, though it usually only attracts our attention in elongated structures, where (that is to say) the radius vector has described a considerable angle.
scope: nails, claws, beaks, incisors, canines and tusks of vertebrates

label: Elephant and American mastodon tusks are the same spiral as the mammoth's, only shorter
claim: The tusks of living elephants and American mastodons follow essentially the same logarithmic spiral as the mammoth's great spiral tusks and differ only in size, so that if they grew long enough they would become equally spiral.
quote: but the American mastodons and the existing species of elephant have tusks which do not differ appreciably, except in size, from the great spiral tusks of the mammoth, though from their comparative shortness the spiral is little developed and only appears to the eye as a gentle curve.
scope: tusks of elephants, mastodons and mammoths (Proboscidea)

label: Spirals of sunflower, thistle and cone are deformations of helices on a stem
claim: The logarithmic spirals of flat or convex inflorescences and the helices on elongated stems are one phenomenon: the fir-cone, teasel, thistle and sunflower heads are successive geometric deformations of a long, nearly cylindrical stem, on which the same arrangement appears as helices.
quote: the semi-ellipsoidal capitulum of the teasel, the more or less hemispherical one of the thistle, and the flattened but still convex one of the sunflower, are all beautiful and successive deformations of what is typically a long, conical, and all but cylindrical stem.
section: Helices and logarithmic spirals in phyllotaxis
scope: leaf, scale and floret arrangements in plants

label: Sunflower spirals intersect isogonally, rarely orthogonally
claim: Against Church, the spirals in a sunflower disc intersect isogonally (at a constant angle), and orthogonal intersection is only a particular and probably infrequent case.
quote: The spirals intersect isogonally, but orthogonal intersection would be only one particular case, and in all probability a very infrequent one, in the intersection of logarithmic spirals developed about a common pole.
scope: parastichies in sunflower capitula and similar inflorescences

label: Phyllotactic spirals follow inevitably from similar parts produced at regular intervals
claim: There is no subtle mystery in phyllotaxis: the steady production of similar parts, similarly placed, at similar successive intervals of time necessarily produces symmetrical patterns (helices on a cylinder, logarithmic spirals on a surface containing the pole), which are a secondary mathematical result rather than a primary phenomenon.
quote: I, for my part, see no subtle mystery in the matter, other than what lies in the steady production of similar growing parts, similarly situated, at similar successive intervals of time.
scope: phyllotaxis of leaves, florets, bracts and scales

label: Parastichy counts on fir-cones are nearly constant within a species
claim: The numbers of conspicuous parastichies on fir-cones are on the whole very constant within a species, e.g. 5 and 3 in the Norway spruce and 8 and 5 in the common larch.
quote: and among fir-cones, we can easily count these, and we find them to be on the whole very constant in number, according to the species.

label: Parastichy numbers change when the structure varies greatly in size
claim: Phyllotactic parastichy numbers vary with the size of the whole structure, as in sunflower discs where one species may show 34/55, 55/89 or even 89/144 rows.
quote: The arrangement, as we have seen, is apt to vary when the entire structure varies greatly in size, as in the disc of the sunflower.
scope: sunflower capitula and other composite inflorescences

label: Right- and left-handed parastichy directions occur about equally often
claim: Within a species, cones with a given parastichy arrangement are nearly equally divided between right-handed and left-handed spiral directions (e.g. 224 versus 243 among 467 Norway spruce cones).
quote: In each case they were nearly equally divided as regards direction; for instance of the 467 cones shewing the five-eight arrangement, the five-series ran in right-handed spirals in 224 cases, and in left-handed spirals in 243.
scope: conifer cones (Norway spruce) and phyllotactic systems generally

label: One Fibonacci parastichy pair necessarily entails all the lower pairs
claim: Following Tait, if a single genetic spiral exists and one pair of parastichy numbers from the series 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… is present, all the lower pairs of the series are necessarily present in the same system.
quote: These are the very series which we have found to be common, or normal; and so far as our investigation has yet gone, it has proved to us that, if one of these exists, it entails, _ipso facto_, the presence of the rest.
scope: spiral phyllotactic systems with a single genetic spiral

label: Most phyllotaxis has between two and three leaves per turn of the genetic spiral
claim: The prevalence of Fibonacci parastichy numbers arises because in the great majority of fir-cones and other phyllotactic systems there are more than two but fewer than three leaves in one turn of the genetic spiral (t = 2); other observed series correspond to t = 3, 4, 5.
quote: And, determined in this manner, it is found in the great majority of cases, in fir-cones and a host of other examples of phyllotaxis, that _t_ = 2.

label: Which parastichies are conspicuous depends on leaf proportions, not on divergence
claim: Which of the implicit spiral families is conspicuous does not depend on the angle of divergence but on the proportions of the leaves or scales, strictly on the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboid circumscribing each leaf-area.
quote: the conspicuousness of one set or another does not depend upon angular divergence. It depends on the relative proportions in length and breadth of the leaves themselves; or, more strictly speaking, on the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboidal figure by which each leaf-area is circumscribed.

label: Convergence of phyllotactic ratios to the golden mean has no biological significance
claim: That the phyllotactic fractions 1/2, 2/3, 3/5… converge to 0.618…, the golden mean, is a mathematical coincidence without biological significance; the precise divergence angle and orthostichies are likewise unimportant.
quote: And lastly, the fact that the successional numbers, expressed as fractions, 1/2, 2/3, 3/5, represent a convergent series, whose final term is equal to 0·61803..., the _sectio aurea_ or “golden mean” of unity, is seen to be a mathematical coincidence, devoid of biological significance
section: Divergence angle and the golden mean

label: Close approximations to the golden mean are rare; poor ones like 2/3 are common
claim: Against the 'ideal angle' theory, phyllotactic arrangements that closely approximate the golden mean (8/13, 13/21, 34/55 and higher) are comparatively rare, while poorer approximations such as 3/5, 2/3 and 1/2 are extremely common.
quote: the arrangements by which a better approximation is got, such as 8/13, 13/21, and the very close approximations such as 34/55, 55/89, 89/144, etc., are comparatively rare, while the much less close approximations of 3/5 or 2/3, or even 1/2, are extremely common.
section: Divergence angle and the golden mean

label: Leaf exposure is changed far more by internode length than by divergence angle
claim: If leaves benefit from being spread apart for exposure to air, lengthening the axis to separate them vertically has a far greater effect than any adjustment of the divergence angle, so the azimuthal 'ideal angle' cannot be the plant's means of optimising exposure.
quote: then it is surely manifest that the simple way to do so is to elongate the axis, and to set the leaves further apart, lengthways on the stem. This has at once a far more potent effect than any nice manipulation of the “angle of divergence.”
section: Divergence angle and the golden mean

label: The Fibonacci series has no adaptive role introduced by natural selection
claim: The Fibonacci series in phyllotaxis, its supposed usefulness, and the hypothesis that natural selection introduced it into plant structure have no place in the study of botanical phenomena.
quote: We come then, without more ado, to the conclusion that the “Fibonacci series,” and its supposed usefulness, and the hypothesis of its introduction into plant-structure through natural selection, are all matters which deserve no place in the plain study of botanical phenomena.
section: Divergence angle and the golden mean

label: Eggs are prolate spheroids, never oblate
claim: Hard-shelled eggs, while often pointed, are never flattened or discoidal: they are prolate, never oblate, solids of revolution.
quote: It is an obvious but by no means negligible fact that the egg, while often pointed, is never flattened or discoidal; it is a prolate, but never an oblate, spheroid.
scope: eggs of birds, tortoises and crocodiles

label: The most pointed eggs are those largest relative to the parent bird
claim: As a very common rule, the most asymmetrical, posteriorly tapered eggs are those that are large relative to the parent bird (guillemot, curlews, sandpipers, terns), because they are under the greatest pressure in the oviduct; relatively large but symmetrical eggs (apteryx) imply a relatively large oviduct.
quote: It can be shown, at least as a very common rule, that those eggs which are most unsymmetrical, or most tapered off posteriorly, are also eggs of a large size relatively to the parent bird.

label: A pullet's first eggs are smaller and rounder than its later ones
claim: In the domestic fowl egg size and shape are directly related: a young pullet's first eggs are smaller and more nearly spherical than later ones, and breeds laying relatively smaller eggs lay rounder eggs.
quote: In the case of the common fowl we can trace a direct relation between the size and shape of the egg, for the first eggs laid by a young pullet are usually smaller, and at the same time are much more nearly spherical than the later ones

label: Peristaltic pressure behind the egg's middle makes the front blunt and rear pointed
claim: Peristaltic contraction of the oviduct applies greatest pressure behind the middle of the forming egg, making the anterior end broader and the posterior narrower; the resulting tapered form also favours movement down the oviduct blunt end first.
quote: from the nature and direction of motion of the peristaltic wave the pressure will be greatest somewhere behind the middle of the egg; in other words, the tube is converted for the time being into a more conical form, and the simple result follows that the anterior end of the egg becomes the broader and the posterior end the narrower.

label: Egg shape is caused by radial pressure of the oviduct before the shell hardens
claim: The essential cause of the form and variation of form of an egg is the regularly varying, largely radial pressure applied by successive rings of the oviduct before the shell solidifies, not adaptation to nesting circumstances.
quote: this factor, the unknown but regularly varying, largely radial, pressure applied by successive annuli of the oviduct, is the essential cause of the form, and variations of form, of the egg.
scope: birds' eggs and other hard-shelled eggs

label: Egg form obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P, the equation of all eggs
claim: The shape of an egg, as an extensible membrane filled with incompressible fluid under external pressure, obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P (external normal pressure plus membrane tension times total curvature equals internal pressure), which Thompson calls the equation of all eggs.
quote: In fact, in so far as the postulates correspond near enough to actualities, the above equation is the equation of _all eggs_ in the universe.

label: Membrane tension peaks at the small end, where abnormal eggs are irregular
claim: In conical eggs with spherical ends, the tension of the envelope is greatest at and near the small end, so that is where eggs are most likely to be distorted or to burst and where abnormal eggs most often show irregularities.
quote: further, that the tension _T_ is greatest at and near the small end of the egg. It is here, in short, that the egg is most likely to be irregularly distorted or even to burst, and it is here that we most commonly find irregularities of shape in abnormal eggs.
scope: birds' eggs, especially pointed eggs and abnormal hen's eggs

label: Lateral spine of Schistosoma eggs is moulded in the ootype, not a species mark
claim: Following Looss, the lateral spine of some Schistosoma eggs is moulded mechanically in a funnel-shaped part of the uterus, so lateral- and terminal-spined eggs are mechanical variants of one thing and do not show the existence of a separate species, S. mansoni.
quote: It ascribes to a mechanical cause a curious peculiarity of form; it shews, by reference to this mechanical principle, that two conditions which were very different to the systematic naturalist’s eye, were really only two simple mechanical modifications of the same thing; and it destroys the chief evidence for the existence of a supposed new species of worm
scope: eggs of Schistosoma haematobium and S. mansoni
